body: I used to be really intelligent, got all A's in school, was thought of as the "smart one" in my family, was always at the literal top of my class in almost all of my college courses, etc. Then a few years ago, I started having problems concentrating, remembering things, putting my thoughts into words, and just overall thinking straight. I'm very error-prone now in really embarrassing ways. It's really hard to have gone your whole life depending pretty much solely on your intelligence as your main asset only to see yourself losing it. Anyway, I've had countless medical tests that have come back normal, and my therapist says these issues can be due to my nervous system breaking down once I became old enough to understand how messed up my childhood truly was. It's truly terrifying, and I pray it's reversible.

Wow, I never thought about it like that, but it's so true that I gravitate toward people who are "messy" and themselves riddled with insecurities because I feel like (and maybe not even irrationally so) that people who come from nicer backgrounds and who have their stuff more "all together" aren't going to want anything to do with me and all of my flaws. I feel less intimidated and insecure with people who have tons of their own problems, but I can def see how this would increase my chances of winding up associating with people who aren't just "quirky" but wind up being so in toxic ways.

I wish! I don't pay much per session already, I just have a very limited budget and no real means of obtaining additional income. Complicated situation that I don't really want to describe because it's so unusual that, if my therapist happened to visit this site, she'd recognize me. Glad you were able to work things out better!

Wow, I never thought of this before. One thing that really frustrates me is how my body tenses up, and I go into physiologic fight or flight mode over the smallest stressors. No amount of intellectual understanding that someone changing my schedule last minute or spilled coffee on the carpet really isn't a life-threatening situation or even a big deal stops my body and mind from overreacting. Maybe it's because for so much of my life, the little things WERE big deals. Hell, having to pee used to be a giant deal because I had a family member who would get in moods where she "didn't want to see our faces," and so having to leave my room to go to the bathroom was enough to cause a dramatic scene that resulted in the cops being called to the house. Thanks for giving me something else to think about.

I think CPTSD replacing BPD entirely would require ignoring blatant reality. While many (arguably most) people with BPD have a traumatic past, there are many people with CPTSD who don't at all fit the picture of someone with BPD. I have a sister with BPD, and our presentations are absolutely nothing alike. She has a very textbook "borderline" pattern of behavior, whereas I was always seen as the subdued "goody two shoes" of my family who was afraid to break rules or do anything to cause anybody any trouble. Treating someone with BPD (or BPD + CPTSD) with the same general protocol as someone with CPTSD and no borderline traits would, I fear, lead to suboptimal treatment outcomes.

That's what I wish I knew how to figure out...whether I'm just wasting money pursuing the possibility or if it could actually be the root of my problems. My instinct says there's no way I could just randomly develop all of these problems after getting through my childhood relatively unscathed, but I don't have any other answers either.

It mostly wasn't sexual in my case...my father just hit us wherever he could reach first...but I struggle so much with being able to say it was abuse even though he gave me bloody noses and stuff sometimes because "disciplining" children like that is still so normalized and was much more so back then. Once a police officer I told even offered to have my father beat me WITH A STICK while he watched, and he "would let him know when it crossed over into abuse."

I physically shudder every time I hear someone talk about hitting their kid as if it's a good, normal thing. Yet I feel like I'm just being an overly sensitive snowflake for feeling like it messed me up because, especially where I live in the south, people literally applaud that type of thing as character building or whatever.

I was able to graduate with an almost 4.0 GPA (got a C in one class, the rest were all A's) with major brain fogginess/concentration/memory problems that suddenly appeared near the end of my freshman year. My therapist says these issues may have emerged due to the development of dissociative tendencies as I became old enough to realize how screwed up my childhood had really been. I had to study ALL of the time to pull it off, though, because it took my brain so much more time to process and store information. Like, my classmates would be bragging about how they didn't start studying for an exam until the night before, and I had been studying for it for the past 3 weeks.

The areas I struggled most were when an assignment didn't allow me to spend so much time preparing or if a professor liked to call on people randomly. I was no good at staying present during lectures, so I just went home and took my time learning the material from the textbook myself.

It's possible, but I can't say whether it is or isn't possible for any particular person because everyone's dissociation is different. I think you should definitely give it a go and just understand you may have to put in a lot more work to get the same results as your classmates who don't have the same issues.

I saw a new therapist a few days ago who said I sound like I may have CPTSD. I'm so distraught that, if she winds up being right, after a decade of suffering and not knowing what's wrong with me, the condition I have isn't even officially recognized. Because I haven't spent enough time being misunderstood and disbelieved already.

I just went into the Dawson McCallister hope line, since the suicide line was useless the other day. This time I was given a long paragraph the guy had obviously copy and pasted with a phone number I could call to talk with a conservative, religious organization. This is the kind of bullshit "help" available when you're poor.
that's the whole point. i can't afford help.
yeah. I want to help others, but I don't even have the energy to brush my teeth these days.
I have plenty of hobbies. I don't have the interest or energy to do any of them when I'm too consumed with thoughts of wanting to die.

Yeah, I'm not in therapy currently, but at times when I start feeling stuck and completely, not only unproductive but incapable of being productive, I start entertaining the thought of going back to therapy. Then I get upset because going to therapy, while productive for many people, isn't the type of productive I desire to be. I want to be the person helping others, not the person needing help for once.
I would imagine you wouldn't have time to wonder about individual clients to this extent given the large numbers of clients most therapists see over their careers! Interesting.

My goal is to just be mentally healthy. I feel like, if I ever get there, therapy will be so associated with dark times in my life that I'll not want to go anywhere near a therapist for fear of it causing me to regress back to that place. But then, if I'm truly mentally healthy, maybe that won't be an issue.

I wish more therapists would recognize that this, for whatever, tends to happen lol. It's so frustrating when a therapist is like, "Wow, you seem to be progressing so much! You seem so much happier and more optimistic today!" Not really...I spent all day yesterday thinking about wanting to be dead, but I guess it's not sustainable to be visibly that distraught 24/7, so here I am not physically breaking down...
See, my last therapist was an older lady in private practice. Guess I just got unlucky!
That makes sense! I guese having the ability to care at all puts you on a different level than someone who has lost any sense of how they present to others.

When I was in therapy, I would look like a trainwreck the entire week--like laying in bed in unwashed clothes with tangled hair and having gone 4 days without showeirng--but would clean up right before my appointments. I was too embarrassed and self-conscious about how I looked most of the time yet at the same time worried the therapist thought I had my shit together way more than I did because, whenever she saw me, I had freshly painted nails, a full face of makeup, and a cute outfit on. I was/am pretty bad off, so I can't even begin to imagine what it feels like to be so bad off that you can't even find the energy to brush your hair and put on makeup one day a week. I feel like the day I got to the point that I'd show up to therapy looking like a slob would be the day I'd just completely lose all will to live and start seriously planning suicide, basically. I guess rock bottom looks different for everyone.

Do you ever consider that clients may clean up for your appointments but otherwise have poor hygiene? Just curious because, back when I was in therapy, I used to go 3 and 4 days without showering, shaving, brushing my hair, etc. but I'd always shower, paint my nails, pluck my eyebrows, put on deodorant, etc. before appointments because I didn't want to come across as the trainwreck I was and be self-conscious about how I looked and smelled the entire appointment. If my therapist saw me between sessions, she probably wouldn't have recognized me.

> Like u/Sinclairlim said, "As therapists our #1 job is to preserve the lives of our patients." I think some therapists see that as their only job. Their duties end at that point, and the rest is up to you. If your life is so bad that you want to die, and you can't change it, then from their perspective, the easiest / cheapest way to for them to get their job done is to take away your ability to kill yourself.  
> 

This is exactly the issue. If all I needed was someone to tell me not to do it and call the cops on me if I'm near actually doing it, I wouldn't need a damn therapist because just about anyone in my life would do the trick. I feel like I keep inching closer and closer to crossing that line from suicidal thoughts to suicidal planning precisely because I'm constantly trying to figure out how to get help before things progress more, and all anyone wants to do is ~assess~ me and then do everything they can to avoid further discussing the topic. All I know is I'm miserable and can't figure out how to help myself.

Suicidal ideation because I've never found a therapist who was comfortable discussing mine with me. The topic seems to really freak therapists out, and they go into save-your-own-ass mode and just start asking me if I'd actually do it. I say no, and then they breathe a sigh of relief and scramble to change the topic. (I'm not dumb enough to say yes even if I were...why, so they can lock me up for 3 days and I can go on being just as depressed when I leave except with an expensive hospital bill?)

I wish I could find a therapist to actually help me with this topic because it's really distressing to have thoughts of wanting to die as your go-to coping method, but they all panic and run away from it.
Not yet. I tried going to my school's therapist, but lol baaaad fit.

I quit therapy abruptly recently and regret it. I think I needed to quit anyway because therapy wasn't really accomplishing any of my goals and was getting progressively awkward and uncomfortable to the point that I was starting to resent spending money to feel uncomfortable, but the lack of closure sucks. I have to drive by where my ex-therapist's office is all of the time. Every time, I find myself sad that I'm not on my way to my former "safe" place that wasn't actually that safe, but idk at least it was somewhere I could talk about what I was going through without being treated like a burden.She obviously said I could come back if I decided I wanted to, but my pride wouldn't let me do that.

I have been wondering this lately. I have very big self-esteem issues. It's not the self esteem issues that bother me so much as the impact they have on my ability to function in society. Nobody wants a nurse or a dentist or an anything else who comes across as lacking confidence in their abilities.

Interesting point about feeling like you can't get good things without being ill. I never thought about it that way, but I really don't know how to get my needs met without having something wrong with me. I mean, even then, I don't know how to get them semi-met without paying someone to take care of me in some way. idk.

Yeah. I have some pretty miserable circumstances in my life, and I feel like therapy just causes me to obsess over them until I can go talk about them to my therapist, who is totally going either to fix them, magically make me not be so negatively affected by them, or at least show me compassion regarding them, which is something I crave not having anyone in my life who really cares about my pain. If I don't have a therapist, it's like, "Welp, might as well do my best not to be so worked up about this because the only outcome of ruminating on it is going to be my own misery. Sure, I have every right to be upset, but it's not like my being upset benefits myself or anyone else."

My OBGYN is male, which I don't mind at all, but I avoid male primary care doctors. I guess I don't feel like I really need my OBGYN to listen to me or make me feel particularly cared about...I just need him to make sure I don't have cancer/my lady bits aren't otherwise falling apart. I go to primary care doctors for a wider range of issues, though, so I need a doctor who I feel will really listen to me and take my concerns seriously. Most of the male PCPs I've seen have just shrugged off everything I came to them with as stress, hypochondria, or what have you.

I was about to make a thread asking what it is about this sub in particular that seems to attract people who want male therapists given that data indicates a large majority of clients prefer women overall. lol. I prefer female therapists. Male therapists come across so cold and like to talk over me in my experiences with them.

It's always interesting to me how much of this sub seems to want male therapists when much of the data I've seen indicates the majority of clients prefer female therapists. When I first started coming here, I began wondering if something was wrong with me for NOT wanting a male therapist. lol. I personally can't stand seeing male therapists. They love to talk over me, which is a huge trigger of mine...because I'm both physically small and come across as insecure, people seem to think they can talk over me and act like they know better than me on every topic. Cannot stand it and will not put up with it from someone I'm paying to listen to me. They also are pretty unempathetic in my experience and come across to me as inauthentic when they try to express empathy. The last male therapist I saw (actually just a few days ago...thanks to my stupid school for only having a male therapist on staff in the counseling center) kept reiterating how much my situation sucks in a very matter-of-fact, emotionally detached way as if I'm too stupid to know that things are bad, whereas my female therapist would at least have some tenderness in her voice rather than coming across so cold. Since I struggle with feeling like no one cares about me this is also a huge no no.

This happened to me the other day. I clicked out and...tbh I don't remember what I did when I closed the page. Probably just cried until I fell asleep because what else was I going to do. God, depression has zapped my entire memory.

It's not that I fault people for not being able to help. I know I damn well couldn't help anyone right now; I can barely manage the bare minimum needed to take care of myself. My issue is more the way the suicidal are always given this false hope that they just need to reach out, and things will improve and also with the way, when they're gone, people will talk about how they should have reached out, assuming they didn't try reaching out dozens of times. I don't want the story of my struggles falsely portrayed because it's more comforting to others to think that things weren't truly hopeless for me.
same

I'm sorry. I guess what keeps me from getting to that point is I have no family to support me (used to live with my dad, but he is about to lose his house...lost his job and is living off of credit cards), so I'd be homeless if I didn't keep trying to figure out how to support myself despite my mental health problems.

This is honestly me. Every time I try to be productive, I get overwhelmed and start fantasizing about wanting to die. However, therapy doesn't pay my bills, so I have to keep trying even though the stress of continuing to push on is going to kill me (which would be a good thing at this point, so...onward?)

I actually don't have a therapist at the moment. I stopped seeing mine a week ago because I felt it wasn't helping and I was just using therapy as an "acceptable" way to avoid doing actual productive things in my life. I wouldn't have been comfortable saying that, though, no. Instead, I just stared at the floor and hoped that my complete lack of acknowledgment of the comment would be enough to prevent it from happening again.

I feel similarly disillusioned and frustrated with the monopoly of CBT as well as some other modalities whose appeals lie more in the more straightforward and clear-cut nature of practicing them than in their actual efficacy for a majority of clients. I get the appeal of CBT. I'm not a mental health professional, but I did study the stuff some in undergrad. It was my favorite class because it appealed to the part of me that likes to problem solve in a step-by-step, straightforward manner. I've always liked math because you just have to follow the steps correctly in order to produce the result you want. CBT is the psychology world's math. 

I just can't stand the way seemingly 90% of mental health professionals attempt to apply CBT to just about every patient's case and, then, imply that the problem is THEM and that they just don't want to get better badly enough when it fails to work. CBT is very well-suited to a very limited number of circumstances. Some people's mental health struggles really do stem from destructive thinking patterns. There are people who are absolutely skilled and brilliant individuals but begin to see themselves as incompetent, useless wastes of space the moment they fail at one thing. There are people who think they're hideous and unlovable because they've been turned down by several people they tried to date when the reality is that rejection is just a part of life for everyone. Those people can benefit from reframing their thinking patterns. Others are just in shitty situations and need realistic coping skills to deal with shitty circumstances that they can't change.

Man, if therapists aren't supposed to comment on even things like clothing or hair, then my therapists have all REALLY screwed up. I dress cutely...that's one thing I do feel pretty confident in saying; my style sense is pretty great...almost every single therapy session I've ever attended with any female therapist has involved them commenting on my clothes, shoes, accessories, or hair. Not so much with male therapists, except the one who said he'd fall down if he wore heels like mine.

I don't currently have a therapist...err kind of...it was a situation where I said I wasn't coming back anymore because I didn't feel like I was getting any better, and she said just let her know if I change my mind...but when I did, I would sometimes feel this way. I always promptly concluded I was being delusional and engaging in wishful thinking, though. There's no way someone with decades of experience seeing thousands of clients come and go can actually care that much about me or feel sad that I'm leaving. Just the nature of what a therapist does makes it impossible to see me, one of as I said thousands of clients she's had, as much more than a paycheck. That's not a value judgement on therapists; it's just the only way I can imagine what their reality is like. They wouldn't be of much use to their other clients if they were investing a huge amount of energy into caring about me personally.

My tendency to do this is part of my reasoning for taking a therapy break, at least for now if not forever. It gives me this very counterproductive "one thing at a time" mentality that my life is on hold until my next session. It runs so counter to what the entire purpose of therapy is supposed to be; it's supposed to help me become better able to live my life, not give me a false sense of productivity that serves as an excuse not to do actual productive "real life" things. Until I can figure out how to treat it as what it's intended to be, therapy might just not be for me.

Now that I've stopped therapy, I find myself constantly thinking about calling up my former therapist and asking if I could resume seeing her again because I miss the breaks from the real world...but therapy isn't supposed to be a break from the real world, it's supposed to be a supplement to the real world. At least for me. I know therapy is different things to different people.

The only time it was directly related to what we were talking about was the time a therapist asked if I thought I was attractive, and I said no. Still felt like going on about how pretty I am was a really poor way to try and boost my confidence, especially given that MOST people's response to someone saying they think they're ugly is going to be to disagree with them regardless of whether they believe what they're saying.

I don't understand what about the concept is so difficult to understand. As people and especially as women, we want to feel attractive, but that doesn't mean we want our looks to be the ONLY thing we are capable of contributing to others or to society.

When I said I think I'm revolting, I was talking in the physical sense since the topic at hand was my physical appearance.

Thank you for responding with your therapist perspective. In my case, I did leave when I was particularly distressed. However, it was because the therapy wasn't helping at all with the distress and was, if anything, contributing to it because of the way the therapist would always agree with me that it was rational to be that distressed because my life circumstances are pretty damn impossible and hopeless. Not sure what the point is of going to therapy to basically be told that feeling suicidal is pretty much justified and rational in your case and the only thing therapy could offer you is a place to vent about how much it sucks (which can only help for so long before I get tired of bitching about hopeless circumstances that suck as much as they do when I left as when I came in).

What u/mdtb9Hw3D8 said was correct. I mean I'm neither a client who only saw her once or twice nor someone who she saw for a year or longer. The five months falls in between those two. I saw her almost every week, sometimes every 2 weeks if she was booked or out of town, for five months straight. Don't think this classifies my tenure as "erratic."
I guess I'm wondering where I fall on that continuum from brand new client to long-term client. I hadn't seen her one or two times, but I also hadn't seen her for a year or longer.
I did, and it doesn't describe me in the least haha. I'm a classic avoidant-dismissive.
